extracted.intended_audience: early 18th-century literate public / readers of The Spectator
extracted.subtask_description: A short moral and social essay (Spectator-style) offering observations, anecdotes, and prescriptive remarks about manners, religion, superstition, and rural life for a general readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Younger sons and employment
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Will. Wimble's is the Case of many a younger Brother of a great Family, who had rather see their Children starve like Gentlemen, than thrive in a Trade or Profession that is beneath their Quality.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument that younger sons should be placed in trade or honest industry rather than maintaining an idle gentlemanly life: trading nations allow younger sons to rise by industry; example of Will Wimble's handicrafts and usefulness contrasted with worthless gentility; compare with earlier 'Twenty first Speculation' for reinforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of small industrious social services
rubrics_metrics.description: 'These Gentleman-like Manufactures and obliging little Humours, make _Will_. the Darling of the Country.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small useful skills (making may-flies, nets, garters, setting-dogs) and obliging behaviours (giving tulip-roots, exchanging poppies, carrying presents) are socially valuable and win civil esteem; examples from Will Wimble's behaviour and the social receptions he receives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dress conveys social and political effect
rubrics_metrics.description: 'It is, said he, worth while to consider the Force of Dress; and how the Persons of one Age differ from those of another, merely by that only.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dress affects perception and has practical/political effects (e.g., Yeomen of the Guard's jetting coat makes them appear taller and more terrible); use portraits and fashions to read historical character and social role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrity, punctuality, and secret charity as gentlemanly virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: 'This Man ... I take to be the Honour of our House. Sir HUMPHREY DE COVERLEY; he was in his Dealings as punctual as a Tradesman, and as generous as a Gentleman.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Punctuality in dealings, keeping one's word, avoiding employments that tempt ambition, industrious husbandry, and giving surplus wealth in secret bounties are exemplary traits; concrete portrait of ancestor who served country, maintained integrity, and used superfluous fortune for friends and neighbours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critique of wit and indolence without justice or industry
rubrics_metrics.description: 'He was one of those that had too much Wit to know how to live in the World; he was a Man of no Justice, but great good Manners; he ruined every Body that had any thing to do with him... he was every way the finest Gentleman in the World.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good manners and wit are insufficient if unaccompanied by justice, prudence, and industry; anecdote of an ancestor whose indolence and mismanagement left debt despite social graces as a warning against valuing style over substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for popular testimony about apparitions (prudence in unbelief)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'If any Man thinks these Facts incredible, let him enjoy his own Opinion to himself, but let him not endeavour to disturb the Belief of others, who by Instances of this Nature are excited to the Study of Virtue.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges widespread historical and contemporary reports of apparitions (historians, poets, philosophers) and argues against aggressively dismissing others' beliefs; includes Josephus story and reference to Lucretius and Locke to show complexity of evidence and psychological causes (association of ideas).

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychology of superstition: association of ideas creates fear
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to Locke: 'The Ideas of Goblins and Sprights have really no more to do with Darkness than Light: Yet let but a foolish Maid inculcate these often on the Mind of a Child, and raise them there together... Darkness shall ever afterwards bring with it those frightful Ideas.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superstition often arises from associative learning and prejudice of education; small natural stimuli (rustling, a cow) can be construed as ghosts by weak or suggestible minds; use as explanation for reports of hauntings and apparitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical remedy for local superstition (ritual/administrative action)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The Knight ... ordered [all the Apartments] to be flung open, and _exorcised_ by his Chaplain, who lay in every Room one after another, and by that Means dissipated the Fears which had so long reigned in the Family.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Community rituals and decisive local leadership (opening rooms, having chaplain perform rites) are presented as effective methods to dispel fears and restore normal use of space; example of Sir Roger restoring order in his house.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keeping Sunday (the Sabbath) civilizes and polishes society
rubrics_metrics.description: 'I am always very well pleased with a Country _Sunday_; and think, if keeping holy the Seventh Day were only a human Institution, it would be the best Method that could have been thought of for the polishing and civilizing of Mankind.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weekly communal observance brings people together in their best habits, refreshes religious notions, encourages civility and sociability; country Sundays enable parish politics, display of best persons, discussion of duties, and general moral upkeep.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local gentry's role in church order and moral encouragement
rubrics_metrics.description: 'As Sir ROGER is Landlord to the whole Congregation, he keeps them in very good Order... he gave every one of them a Hassock and a Common-prayer Book: and at the same time employed an itinerant Singing-Master... he has promised upon the Death of the present Incumbent, who is very old, to bestow it according to Merit.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical steps gentry should take: provide prayerbooks and hassocks, fund music instruction, reward children (Bibles, bacon) for catechism, add to clerk's stipend, and promise incumbency by merit — measures that enforce decorum and encourage piety and meritocracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feuds between squire and parson harm the common people
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The next Village is famous for the Differences and Contentions that rise between the Parson and the 'Squire... Matters are come to such an Extremity, that the 'Squire has not said his Prayers either in publick or private this half Year; and that the Parson threatens him, if he does not mend his Manners, to pray for him in the Face of the whole Congregation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public disputes between local elites (wealth vs learning) produce social harm: tenants adopt atheism or tithe-stealing; truth is discounted when wealthy men are openly irreligious; thus local leaders should avoid such feuds to preserve parish morals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immortality of the soul as moral foundation (perpetual progress argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Among these and other excellent Arguments for the Immortality of the Soul, there is one drawn from the perpetual Progress of the Soul to its Perfection... How can it enter into the Thoughts of Man, that the Soul, which is capable of such immense Perfections... shall fall away into nothing almost as soon as it is created?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presents multiple arguments for immortality: (1) nature/immateriality of soul; (2) passions and love of existence; (3) nature of the Supreme Being; and (4) the soul's endless capacity for improvement — the last offered as a novel and strong moral argument implying life-after-life that grounds virtue and hope.
